text: Fill in the missing targeting molecule, signal or compartment for each disorder.
questions: An infant with coarse facies, gum hypertrophy and stiff joints has lysosomal enzymes that lack the *mannose-6-phosphate/M6P:This sugar-phosphate address label is added by a phosphotransferase in the cis-Golgi.* tag and are found at high levels in the plasma.

A floppy newborn with seizures, hepatomegaly and renal cysts has PEX gene mutations that prevent protein import into *peroxisomes:These single-membrane organelles contain catalase and oxidise very-long-chain fatty acids.*.

A child with recurrent calcium oxalate kidney stones has alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase mistargeted to *mitochondria:This double-membraned organelle has cristae and its own DNA — the wrong destination for this enzyme.* instead of peroxisomes.
Escaped ER-resident proteins are retrieved from the cis-Golgi by receptors that recognise their C-terminal *KDEL:A four-letter code at the C-terminus that signals 'return to the ER'.* sequence.

Without a functional signal peptide, a protein cannot be recognised by the *signal recognition particle/SRP:This RNA–protein complex pauses translation and directs the ribosome to the ER membrane.* and remains in the cytosol.

overallFeedback.feedback: Each targeting disorder arises when a normal protein reaches the wrong compartment: without the mannose-6-phosphate tag, lysosomal enzymes are secreted (I-cell disease); without PEX-mediated import, peroxisomes remain empty (Zellweger); a misdirecting signal sends the enzyme to mitochondria (PH1). KDEL retrieves escaped ER residents, and the signal recognition particle is essential for co-translational ER entry.
